groundTruthNarrative: The zero-deviation record is a reporting artifact. From 1 February 2026 each deviation report cost the line supervisor 4% of bonus; reports collapsed within weeks while defects did not: independent final-inspection rejections rose on every line, customer complaints nearly tripled, the bond-station CAPA from 2025 was never implemented, and the training program credited by QA started after the drop. Fear of consequences rose sharply and the one hotline report was 'investigated' only by asking the accused supervisor. Line 3, historically the worst line for luer-bond leaks, became the showcase: since June its record output comes from about five technicians borrowed daily off the books from Lines 1 and 4, with productivity per real labor-hour unchanged, while the lending lines fell behind. Line 3 lots dominate the complaints. Whether the complaint surge stems from undocumented rework or from uncertified borrowed technicians, whether the extra material purchases are Line 3 rework or plant-wide, and who authorized the lending are not yet established. The right move is to remove the reporting penalty, protect reporters, and run an independent reconciliation, not to copy Line 3 or punish individuals yet.

answers.rationale: The only evidence for real improvement is the deviation count itself (E1, E2), which the supervisors control and are penalized for (E3). Measures outside the bonus scheme move the other way: independent QC lot rejections rose from 0.8% to 1.3% on all five lines (E12), customer complaint ppm rose from 11 to 31 (E11), and the known bond-station cause was never fixed (E17). The claim is contradicted, not merely unestablished.

Reports fell from about 14 a month to 3 in the month the penalty took effect and then to zero on every line (E2, E3), while the non-incentivized final-inspection reject rate rose on all five lines (E12) and complaints rose (E11). Staff say defects are 'fixed and moved on' without records (E15), fear of raising concerns doubled on all lines (E16), and the hotline report describes unrecorded rework (E8). Underreporting explains every signal; real improvement explains none of the outside measures.

The practices the supervisor cites have been in place since early 2025 (E5), but attainment only jumped in June (E4), exactly when off-book borrowing of about 5.3 technicians a day began (E13). Output per actual technician-hour is unchanged (41.2 vs 40.8 vs 41.0, E13), so there is no productivity advantage to transfer, and Lines 1 and 4 lost attainment in the same window (E4, E14).

The supplier change in April lines up with the rise in complaints, which is a timing trap. But all five lines use the same tubing, yet complaints concentrate in Line 3 lots (71% of complaints, 34% of units) while Lines 2 and 5 contribute only 6 complaints on 31% of units (E11). With a 9-week lag, Q2 complaints concern units built in February-March with the old tubing (E11). Incoming-inspection reject rates for the new tubing are unchanged (E10), and the complaint mode is the bond joint, which was already a known Line 3 problem (E17).

Deviations fell to 3 in February and zero from March (E2), but the training launched on 9 March (E7). Only 40% of technicians had finished it by June, yet every line reported zero from March. Outside quality measures got worse, not better (E12). The QA manager's attribution (E6) does not survive the timing.

The Line 4 supervisor is 'told' to lend people but declines to say by whom (E14). The Plant Manager's claim of 'no extra headcount' (E1) is consistent with being unaware and also with concealment. Closing the hotline case after one conversation (E9) shows a weak investigation, not proven knowledge of the lending. No evidence names who authorizes the lending, so the claim is live but unestablished.

The evidence gives temporal order (policy effective 1 Feb, reports drop that month, E2/E3), a stated mechanism (bonus loss per report, echoed in E8 and E15), and covariation across all five lines. It also gives a built-in control: final-inspection rejects, which are excluded from the incentive, rose instead of falling (E12). Rival explanations are ruled out: training came later (E7) and no process change was made (E17). Together these meet the causal bar.

Borrowing begins the first week of June and Line 3 attainment jumps from 101% to 118% in the same period (E4, E13), while the lending lines fall (Line 4 99% to 91%, Line 1 100% to 95%; E4, E14). Output per real labor-hour is flat, so the extra labor accounts for the extra output almost exactly (E13). The rival explanation, better practices, was already in place before June (E5). Mechanism, timing, covariation and a ruled-out rival together make this causal.

Purchases of exactly the materials re-bonding consumes (connectors, adhesive) rose 30% from February, the same time the penalty began and the time the hotline dates the back-cage rework from (E8, E10), so the two co-occur. But purchases are booked at plant level and not by line (E10). Defects rose on all five lines (E12), so unrecorded rework or scrap could be happening anywhere, and part of the increase is volume (+9%). The link to Line 3 rework specifically is an association, not an established cause.

Line 3 lots and luer-bond leaks dominate complaints, and that fits with re-bonding outside the record (E8, E11). But the rework is alleged, not verified (E8, E15). There are live rivals. The unresolved bond-cure CAPA (E17) combined with suppressed reporting could let defective units escape un-reworked, so suppression rather than rework itself could drive the complaints. From June, uncertified borrowed technicians also work the bond station (E7, E13), which could explain the later (Q3) part of the rise, though not the Q2 rise from February-March builds (E11). No unit-level link exists between reworked units and complained units, so the two co-occur but the causal path is not established.

The timing coincidence is the only support. A common supply input cannot explain why complaints concentrate in one line, and the lag places Q2 complaints on pre-switch production (E11). Incoming inspection shows no quality change in the new tubing (E10). The evidence counts against the link.

Line 3's output comes from hidden borrowed labor (E13), not from better practice, and its lots drive the complaint increase (E11). Raising every line's target to that level cannot be met honestly. It would push all lines toward the same off-book staffing, undocumented rework and silence (E12, E16), which makes product risk worse and deepens concealment.

The penalty is the established cause of the suppression (R1). Removing it, together with an explicit non-retaliation commitment and amnesty, goes straight at the mechanism and at the fear reported on all lines (E15, E16). It restores the information the plant needs to run the investigation. It is reversible and does not depend on any unresolved question.

The only prior inquiry was run inside the accused chain and consisted of one denial (E9). The open questions are rework, who authorized the lending, and which cause drives the complaints (I6, I9, I10). These can only be resolved from records outside the plant's control. Complaints are rising on a medical device (E11), so an independent reconciliation and a risk review of shipped lots is among the best next steps.

The rework allegation is not yet verified (E8, E15). Who directs the lending is unknown, and the lending lines' supervisor implies instructions come from someone else (E14). The supervisor operates under an incentive the plant created (E3). Discipline could be warranted if the investigation confirms personal falsification, but committing to it now runs ahead of the evidence and risks punishing the wrong party first.

The reporter asked for anonymity (E8). The Plant Manager is inside the chain that closed the case without a real inquiry (E9) and that may be directing the lending (I6 unknown). Staff already fear consequences (E15, E16). Unmasking the reporter would break the one working protective channel and invite retaliation, which suppresses information.

The core mechanism, reporting suppression caused by the bonus penalty, is established causally (I7). The hidden-labor basis of Line 3's output is also established (I8). That is enough to commit to a substantive change: removing the penalty and protecting reporters (I13). Open questions about culpability and the exact complaint pathway affect who is held accountable and the corrective detail, not whether to act.
